title: Drought, Household Water Access, and Child Undernutrition: Evidence From Kenya
content:
Abstract

Climate change is putting immense strain on food and water resources, which can have dire health consequences. This is particularly concerning for young children, for whom undernutrition may have lasting social and health effects into adult life. Within the context of a severe long-term drought in the Greater Horn of Africa between late 2020 and early 2023, we examined the relationship between exposure to the drought in Kenya, water access, and child nutritional status. We linked child- and household-level data from the 2022 Kenyan Demographic and Health Survey (DHS) (n = 16,632) with district-level measures of drought exposure defined by the international disaster database (EM-DAT) alongside measures of precipitation and temperature anomalies during the year preceding household surveys. Controlling for household demographics, we used logistic regression analyses to examine the relationship between drought, temperature, precipitation, water access, and three indicators of undernutrition for children under five: underweight, wasted, and stunted. Households who were exposed to the drought had lower odds of at least basic water access. Further, children exposed to the drought had higher odds of being wasted. Sensitivity analyses show consistent results, that increased temperature (both continuous measures and the top quintile of anomalies) was associated with higher odds of a child being wasted. Overall, the historic drought was associated with children's prevalence of undernutrition, highlighting the role of increased temperature. There is a need for future longitudinal research to explore the role of water access in mediating drought effects or improving drought recovery.
